title: Dryope. Iolaus
titleEn: Dryope, and the Years Given Back — Metamorphoses IX.324–417
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Iole tells her mother-in-law Alcmene what became of her half-sister Dryope, who came to a pool with her infant son to bring garlands to the nymphs and picked flowers from a water-lotus that had once been a nymph herself. Bark closes over Dryope while the child is still at her breast, and she gets out her last instructions for him — give him to a nurse, let him play under this tree, let him fear pools and never pick a flower from a tree — before her mouth stops speaking and stops being. The grief is broken off at the door by Iolaus, given back his first years as a gift, and by the goddess Themis, who forbids the giver to swear off such gifts and prophesies the wars and murders that will call for another. Two of the women here are in the tale because a god wanted them: the Latin gives Dryope's rape half a line and Lotis three, and moves on.

advisory.lede: This part carries two sexual assaults: Apollo's rape of Dryope, told in half a line before the story moves on, and Priapus's assault on the nymph Lotis, which she escaped only by ceasing to be a woman.
advisory.more: The Latin gives Dryope's rape half a line — she is “lacking her maidenhood and having suffered the force of the god” — and passes straight on to her marriage, in which her husband is called a lucky man. The phrase vim pati is the ordinary Latin for being raped, and nothing here softens it. Lotis appears for three lines as country hearsay: she fled Priapus, the coarse fertility god of gardens, and escaped by turning into the water-lotus, which is not a rescue but the end of the life she had. That tree is the one Dryope then plucks a flower from, and the grief the tale spends its length on is hers: she loses her own body for it, and Lotis is not heard from again. Lectorium presents the text as written, unaltered, and the notes say plainly what the Latin says.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et admonitu veteris commota ministrae
ingemuit.
sentences.l: She spoke, and, stirred by the recollection of her old serving-woman, she groaned.
sentences.i: So she ended, and the memory of her old serving-woman moved her to a groan.
sentences.n: Dixit closes off the tale the speaker has just been telling. admonitu is an ablative of cause, “by the reminding”, and veteris ministrae is the genitive depending on it: the reminder is of the woman, not by her. ministra is a female servant or attendant.

sentences.t: Quam sic nurus est adfata dolentem:
sentences.l: And her, as she grieved, her son's wife addressed thus:
sentences.i: And her daughter-in-law spoke to her like this in her grief:
sentences.n: Quam is a connecting relative — “and her” — with dolentem agreeing with it: “and her, grieving”. nurus is a son's wife; she is named at line 394. adfata est is from adfor, deponent (passive in form, active in meaning): she did the addressing.

sentences.t:
“Te tamen, o genetrix, alienae sanguine vestro
rapta movet facies.
sentences.l: “Yet it is you, o mother, whom the snatched-away face of a woman not of your blood moves.
sentences.i: “And yet, mother, it is a woman who is no kin of yours whose stolen shape moves you so.
sentences.n: alienae is a genitive depending on facies — “the face of a woman foreign to your blood” — not an adjective agreeing with it; sanguine vestro is the ablative that alienus takes, that is, no relation of yours. rapta, “snatched away”, is the loss of her human shape; the change itself is not told in these lines, and the woman is the old serving-woman of line 324. Magnus prints vestro, “your”; some editions print nostro, “our”, which would put the speaker inside that household instead of outside it.

sentences.t:
Quid si tibi mira sororis
fata meae referam? quamquam lacrimaeque dolorque
impediunt prohibentque loqui.
sentences.l: What if I should tell you the wondrous fate of my own sister? — though tears and grief hinder me and forbid me to speak.
sentences.i: What if I were to tell you my own sister's strange story? — though tears and grief get in the way and will not let me speak.
sentences.n: Quid si with the subjunctive referam is a courteous offer rather than a real question: “suppose I were to tell you”. fata is a neuter plural used of one person's destiny, normal in verse. impediunt prohibentque hang two verbs on the single infinitive loqui — they hinder and forbid her to speak.

sentences.t:
Fuit unica matri
(me pater ex alia genuit) notissima forma
Oechalidum Dryope.
sentences.l: There was her mother's only child — my father begot me of another woman — most famed in beauty of the daughters of Oechalia, Dryope.
sentences.i: Dryope was her mother's only daughter — my father had me by another woman — and the most famous for beauty of all the women of Oechalia.
sentences.n: unica matri: the dative says whose only child she was. The parenthesis makes the two women half-sisters with a father in common, and he is named at line 356 as the child's grandfather. notissima forma is an ablative of respect, “best known in respect of beauty”, and Oechalidum is a Greek genitive plural, “of the women of Oechalia”. The name Dryope is held back to the end of it all.

sentences.t:
Quam virginitate carentem
vimque dei passam Delphos Delumque tenentis
excipit Andraemon, et habetur coniuge felix.
sentences.l: And her, lacking her maidenhood and having suffered the force of the god who holds Delphi and Delos, Andraemon takes to wife, and is counted happy in his bride.
sentences.i: And she — her maidenhood gone, raped by the god who holds Delphi and Delos — is the one Andraemon takes to wife, and he is thought a lucky man in his bride.
sentences.n: Quam is another connecting relative, “and her”, carrying both participles: carentem takes the ablative virginitate, and passam is from patior, deponent (passive in form, active in meaning), “having undergone”. vim pati is the ordinary Latin for being raped, and that is what the phrase says. The god who holds Delphi and Delos is Apollo. excipit is a historic present, and habetur coniuge felix, “is held fortunate in his wife”, sets a husband's good luck straight against what has just been said of her.

sentences.t:
Est lacus adclivis devexo margine formam
litoris efficiens: summum myrteta coronant.
sentences.l: There is a lake sloping up, with its rim shelving down, making the shape of a shore: myrtle-thickets crown its top.
sentences.i: There is a pool whose bank climbs from a shelving edge, so that it curves like a seashore; myrtle thickets ring the top of it.
sentences.n: adclivis is Magnus's spelling, kept as printed. The ground rises away from the water while the margo slopes down into it, and between them the edge takes the curve of a beach — formam litoris efficiens, “making the shape of a shore”. summum is a neuter adjective used as a noun, “the topmost part”, and it is what the myrtles crown.

sentences.t:
Venerat huc Dryope fatorum nescia, quoque
indignere magis, nymphis latura coronas;
sentences.l: Dryope had come here, ignorant of her fates, and — that you may be indignant the more — about to bring garlands to the nymphs;
sentences.i: Dryope had come here knowing nothing of what was fated for her, and — this should make you angrier still — meaning to carry garlands to the nymphs;
sentences.n: quoque here is quo-que, “and by which”, not the adverb “also”: quo with the comparative magis opens a purpose clause, “so that you may be the more indignant”, and indignere is its second-person subjunctive — the teller turning aside to her listener. nescia takes the genitive fatorum. latura is the future participle of fero, “about to carry”: she is bringing the nymphs a gift at the moment she does harm to one of them.

sentences.t:
inque sinu puerum, qui nondum impleverat annum,
dulce ferebat onus tepidique ope lactis alebat.
sentences.l: and in her lap she was carrying a boy who had not yet filled out a year, a sweet burden, and was feeding him with the help of warm milk.
sentences.i: and at her breast she was carrying her boy, not yet a year old — a sweet weight — and keeping him fed with her warm milk.
sentences.n: dulce ... onus stands in apposition to puerum: the child is the sweet burden. impleverat annum, “had filled out a year”, is the Latin way of giving an infant's age. ope lactis is literally “by the help of milk”, a periphrasis for nursing him, and tepidi makes the milk warm from the body — a warmth the following lines take away.

sentences.t:
Haud procul a stagno Tyrios imitata colores
in spem bacarum florebat aquatica lotos.
sentences.l: Not far from the water, copying Tyrian colours, a water-lotus was in flower toward the promise of berries.
sentences.i: Not far from the pool a water lotus was in bloom, its flowers the purple of Tyre, promising the berries to come.
sentences.n: Tyrios colores names the purple of Tyre, the most costly dye there was, so the plant is described by a luxury. in spem bacarum is “into the hope of berries”: the blossom is the fruit's promise, which is part of what makes the plucking of it worse. imitata is from imitor, deponent (passive in form, active in meaning), and its perfect participle has present force here. lotos keeps a Greek feminine nominative.

sentences.t:
Carpserat hinc Dryope, quos oblectamina nato
porrigeret, flores, et idem factura videbar
(namque aderam):
sentences.l: Dryope had plucked from it flowers, which she might hold out to her son as playthings, and I seemed about to do the same (for I was there):
sentences.i: Dryope had picked flowers from it, to hold out to her boy as toys, and I looked as if I would do the same — I was standing right there —
sentences.n: quos ... porrigeret is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive: “flowers to hold out”. oblectamina is a predicate accusative, “as amusements”, and nato the dative, “for her son”. idem factura is a future participle, “about to do the same”. The parenthesis namque aderam is what the whole tale rests on: the teller saw it.

sentences.t:
vidi guttas e flore cruentas
decidere et tremulo ramos horrore moveri.
sentences.l: I saw drops of blood fall from the flower, and the branches be moved with a trembling shudder.
sentences.i: I saw drops of blood fall from the blossom, and the branches stir with a shudder of horror.
sentences.n: vidi governs two accusatives with their infinitives — guttas ... decidere and ramos ... moveri — the ordinary shape of indirect statement after a verb of perceiving. moveri is passive, “be stirred”, so nothing is said about what moves them. tremulo horrore is an ablative of manner, and horror covers both the physical bristling of leaves and the dread of it.

sentences.t:
Scilicet, ut referunt tardi nunc denique agrestes,
Lotis in hanc nymphe, fugiens obscena Priapi,
contulerat versos servato nomine, vultus.
sentences.l: Doubtless — as the country folk report it, slow, and only now at last — the nymph Lotis, fleeing the obscenities of Priapus, had transferred into this plant her turned features, with her name preserved.
sentences.i: The truth was — as the country people tell it, slow to speak, and only now at last — that the nymph Lotis, in flight from Priapus and his obscenity, had passed into this tree her changed face, and kept her name.
sentences.n: tardi is an adjective doing an adverb's work: the neighbours knew, and said nothing until now. Lotis ... nymphe keeps a Greek nominative. obscena is a neuter plural noun, “the obscene things”, of Priapus, the coarse fertility god of gardens: she fled his sexual assault, and escaped it only by ceasing to be a woman. servato nomine is an ablative absolute — the plant is called lotos after her — and the accusative phrase versos ... vultus is split around it.

sentences.t:
Nescierat soror hoc. Quae cum perterrita retro
ire et adoratis vellet discedere nymphis,
haeserunt radice pedes.
sentences.l: My sister had not known this. And when she, terrified, wished to go back and to withdraw, with the nymphs duly worshipped, her feet clung fast by a root.
sentences.i: My sister knew nothing of it. And when in terror she wanted to turn back and go away, her prayers to the nymphs once made, her feet had taken root and held her.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative, “and she”, with cum and the subjunctive vellet giving the circumstance. adoratis ... nymphis is an ablative absolute: she had done everything correctly by the nymphs, which is the cruelty of it. In haeserunt radice pedes the ablative radice is “by a root”, and the verb ends in -erunt where verse often has -ere.

sentences.t:
Convellere pugnat,
nec quicquam nisi summa movet.
sentences.l: She fights to tear herself free, and moves nothing except the topmost parts.
sentences.i: She struggles to wrench herself loose, and nothing but her upper body will move.
sentences.n: pugnat with a plain infinitive, convellere, is a poetic economy where prose would write a purpose clause: “fights to tear away”. summa is a neuter plural used as a noun, “the top parts” — everything above what has already turned to root. The verbs move into the present here and stay there through the change.

sentences.t:
Subcrescit ab imo
totaque paulatim lentus premit inguina cortex.
sentences.l: The bark grows up from the lowest part and slowly, clinging, presses over all her groin.
sentences.i: From below the bark climbs, and little by little, clinging tight, closes over her whole groin.
sentences.n: cortex, the subject, is held back to the last word of its sentence, so the growing and the pressing arrive before the thing that does them. ab imo, “from the lowest part”, answers summa in the line before. lentus carries both its senses at once, slow and clinging, and inguina is a neuter plural for the groin and lower body.

sentences.t:
Ut vidit, conata manu laniare capillos,
fronde manum implevit: frondes caput omne tenebant.
sentences.l: When she saw it, having tried to tear her hair with her hand, she filled her hand with leaf: leaves held her whole head.
sentences.i: When she saw, she tried to tear her hair with her hand and filled her hand with leaf: leaves had taken her whole head.
sentences.n: Ut with the perfect indicative vidit is “when”, not “as though”. conata is from conor, deponent — active in meaning — “having attempted”. The point is carried by the number: fronde is singular, one handful of leaf, and frondes plural is what her head has become.

sentences.t:
At puer Amphissos (namque hoc avus Eurytus illi
addiderat nomen) materna rigescere sentit
ubera, nec sequitur ducentem lacteus umor.
sentences.l: But the boy Amphissos — for his grandfather Eurytus had given him this name — feels his mother's breasts grow stiff, and the milky flow does not follow him as he draws.
sentences.i: But the boy Amphissos — his grandfather Eurytus had given him the name — feels his mother's breasts turn hard, and no milk comes when he pulls.
sentences.n: The parenthesis splits hoc from its noun nomen across the line end, and materna is cut off from ubera in the same way. sentit takes an accusative and infinitive, ubera rigescere. ducentem is an accusative participle, “the one drawing”, and the object of sequitur: the milk will not follow the child pulling at it. This grandfather is the father of line 330 — the teller is called Eurytus's daughter, Eurytidos, at line 395.

sentences.t:
Spectatrix aderam facti crudelis opemque
non poteram tibi ferre, soror;
sentences.l: A watcher I was there, of the cruel deed, and I could not bring help to you, sister;
sentences.i: I stood by and watched that cruelty, and could bring you no help, sister;
sentences.n: spectatrix is the feminine agent-noun, “a woman looking on”, in apposition to the subject of aderam. The tibi and the vocative soror turn the speech aside from the listener to the sister who is gone — an apostrophe, and it lasts no longer than this sentence. Magnus prints facti, “of the deed”, which blames an act; some editions print fati, “of the fate”, which blames a destiny.

sentences.t:
quantumque valebam,
crescentem truncum ramosque amplexa morabar
et, fateor, volui sub eodem cortice condi.
sentences.l: and as far as my strength went, embracing the growing trunk and the branches, I kept trying to hold them back, and — I confess it — I wished to be shut away under the same bark.
sentences.i: and with all the strength I had I threw my arms round the growing trunk and the branches and tried to hold them off, and — I admit it — I wanted to be closed up under the same bark myself.
sentences.n: quantum valebam is “as much as I was strong”. amplexa is from amplector, deponent (passive in form, active in meaning): she does the embracing. morabar is an imperfect of attempt — not “I delayed it” but “I kept trying to delay it”. condi is a passive infinitive, “to be hidden away”, and she wishes it on herself.

sentences.t:
Ecce vir Andraemon genitorque miserrimus adsunt
et quaerunt Dryopen: Dryopen quaerentibus illis
ostendi loton.
sentences.l: See — her husband Andraemon and her most wretched father are there, and they seek Dryope: to them, seeking Dryope, I pointed out the lotus.
sentences.i: And now here are her husband Andraemon and her father in all his misery, and they are asking for Dryope — and to them, asking for Dryope, I showed the lotus tree.
sentences.n: vir here is “husband”, not “man”. The two accusatives Dryopen ... Dryopen stand on either side of the colon: they ask for a woman and are shown a tree. quaerentibus illis is a dative participle, “to them as they sought”. Both Dryopen and loton are accusatives keeping their Greek endings in -n, where Latin forms would have Dryopam and lotum.

sentences.t:
Tepido dant oscula ligno
adfusique suae radicibus arboris haerent.
sentences.l: They give kisses to the warm wood and, flung down at the roots of their own tree, cling there.
sentences.i: They kiss the warm wood, and throw themselves down at the roots of the tree that is theirs, and will not let go.
sentences.n: tepido ligno is a dative after dant: they kiss wood, and it is still warm. adfusi is “poured out upon”, the word for a body thrown down at someone's feet or at an altar. suae ... arboris does the whole recognition in one possessive — the tree is theirs now.

sentences.t:
Nil nisi iam faciem, quod non foret arbor, habebat
cara soror:
sentences.l: Nothing that was not tree did my dear sister now have, except her face:
sentences.i: By this time my dear sister was tree everywhere but her face:
sentences.n: quod picks up nil, not faciem: “nothing which was not tree”. foret is an older equivalent of esset, and the clause is one of characteristic. nisi iam faciem is pushed in ahead of that clause, so the exception arrives before the rule it breaks.

sentences.t:
lacrimae misero de corpore factis
inrorant foliis, et, dum licet oraque praestant
vocis iter, tales effundit in aera questus:
sentences.l: tears bedew the leaves that had been made from her wretched body, and, while it is still allowed and her mouth still affords a road for her voice, she pours out into the air laments like these:
sentences.i: tears wet the leaves that had been made out of her poor body, and while she still may, while her mouth still gives her voice a way out, she pours these laments into the air:
sentences.n: misero de corpore factis belongs with foliis, and the phrase straddles the verse end — factis closes one line and foliis stands early in the next, with the verb between them. inrorant, “bedew”, is from ros, dew, and takes the dative foliis: the tears fall on leaves made out of the body that weeps them. ora praestant vocis iter makes speech a road, which is what the closing bark is about to shut.

sentences.t:
“Siqua fides miseris, hoc me per numina iuro
non meruisse nefas: patior sine crimine poenam.
sentences.l: “If there is any belief given the wretched, I swear by the divine powers that I have not deserved this horror: I suffer a punishment without a crime.
sentences.i: “If the wretched are believed at all, I swear by the gods that I have not earned this outrage: I bear a punishment though I did nothing wrong.
sentences.n: siqua is si qua, “if any”, and fides miseris has the dative, “trust for the wretched”. iuro takes an accusative and infinitive, me ... non meruisse, and hoc is separated from its noun nefas by the line end. patior is deponent (passive in form, active in meaning), “I undergo”. The antithesis of poenam against sine crimine is the whole of her defence, and nothing in these lines answers it.

sentences.t:
Viximus innocuae: si mentior, arida perdam
quas habeo, frondes et caesa securibus urar.
sentences.l: We have lived harmless: if I lie, may I lose, withered, the leaves I have, and, felled by axes, be burned.
sentences.i: I have lived without harming anyone: if I am lying, let me wither and lose the leaves I have, and be cut down with axes and burned.
sentences.n: innocuae is a nominative plural where one woman is speaking — the poetic plural for “I”, which viximus matches. arida and caesa are both feminine singular and agree with her, so the curse she calls down falls on the body she now has. perdam and urar can each be read as future indicative (“I shall lose ... I shall be burned”) or as present subjunctive (“may I lose ... may I be burned”); the forms do not decide it, and the shape of an oath wants the wish. The object frondes stands after the relative clause that describes it, quas habeo.

sentences.t:
Hunc tamen infantem maternis demite ramis
et date nutrici; nostraque sub arbore saepe
lac facitote bibat nostraque sub arbore ludat!
sentences.l: This infant, though, take from his mother's branches and give him to a nurse; and beneath our tree see to it that he often drinks milk, and beneath our tree that he plays!
sentences.i: But take this baby off his mother's branches and give him to a nurse — and see that he drinks his milk often under our tree, and plays under our tree!
sentences.n: maternis ... ramis is an ablative of separation, and “his mother's branches” is plain fact here rather than a figure. facitote is the future imperative of facio, “see to it”, and it governs the bare subjunctives bibat and ludat with no ut between. The repeated nostra sub arbore is the refrain of the speech: she is asking to go on being his mother as a tree.

sentences.t:
Cumque loqui poterit, matrem facitote salutet,
et tristis dicat “latet hoc in stipite mater.”
sentences.l: And when he shall be able to speak, see to it that he greets his mother, and sadly says “my mother lies hidden in this trunk.”
sentences.i: And when he can talk, see that he gives his mother her greeting, and says sadly: “my mother is hidden in this trunk.”
sentences.n: poterit is future, “when he shall be able”. facitote governs salutet and dicat just as before. tristis is a nominative adjective doing adverbial work: “sad, let him say”. stipes is the stock or trunk of a tree, a heavier word than arbor, and the inner quotation marks are Magnus's own.

sentences.t:
Stagna tamen timeat nec carpat ab arbore flores,
et frutices omnes corpus putet esse deorum!
sentences.l: Yet let him fear pools, and not pluck flowers from a tree, and let him think all shrubs are the body of gods!
sentences.i: But let him be afraid of standing water, and never pick flowers off a tree, and let him believe every bush is a god's body!
sentences.n: timeat, carpat and putet are jussive subjunctives — “let him ...”. corpus ... esse deorum is an accusative and infinitive after putet, and corpus stays singular against the plural frutices. The warning is drawn straight from what has just happened to her, so her death becomes a rule the child must live by. Magnus prints deorum, “of gods”; some editions print dearum, “of goddesses”, which would point the warning at the two women of this tale.

sentences.t:
Care vale coniunx, et tu, germana, paterque!
Qui, siqua est pietas, ab acutae vulnere falcis,
a pecoris morsu frondes defendite nostras.
sentences.l: Farewell, dear husband, and you, sister, and father! And you, if there is any family duty in you, defend my leaves from the wound of the sharp pruning-hook, from the bite of the flock.
sentences.i: Dear husband, farewell; and you, my sister; and you, father! And all three of you, if you have any love for your own, keep my leaves from the wound of the sharp pruning-hook and from the teeth of the grazing flock.
sentences.n: Qui at the head of the next sentence is a connecting relative picking up the three people just addressed — “and you who” — and it takes the imperative defendite. pietas is the loyalty owed inside a family, not “pity”. falx is the curved blade of the pruner, and a pecoris morsu is the flock cropping the leaves: the two ways a tree dies, by hand and by mouth.

sentences.t:
Et quoniam mihi fas ad vos incumbere non est,
erigite huc artus et ad oscula nostra venite,
dum tangi possunt, parvumque attollite natum.
sentences.l: And since it is not permitted me to lean down to you, raise your bodies up here and come to my kisses, while they can be touched, and lift up my little son.
sentences.i: And since heaven does not allow me to bend down to you, stretch up to me and come to my lips while they can still be touched — and lift my little boy up to me.
sentences.n: fas est is what divine law allows, a heavier word than licet. incumbere ad vos is “to lean over towards you”: she cannot move, so the living have to do the moving, which is what erigite huc artus asks of them. Magnus prints possunt, so it is the kisses that can still be touched; some editions print possum, “while I can be touched”.

sentences.t:
Plura loqui nequeo. Nam iam per candida mollis
colla liber serpit, summoque cacumine condor.
sentences.l: I cannot speak more. For already the soft bark creeps over my white neck, and I am being buried in the topmost crown.
sentences.i: I can say no more. Already the soft inner bark is creeping over my white throat, and I am being covered over in the very top of the tree.
sentences.n: liber is the inner bark of a tree, the layer written on, and so the word behind “library”. mollis is split from liber and candida from colla by the line end, so both phrases straddle the verse. condor is passive, “I am being hidden away”, and it is the last thing she is able to say about herself.

sentences.t:
Ex oculis removete manus: sine munere vestro
contegat inductus morientia lumina cortex!”
sentences.l: Take your hands away from my eyes: without any service of yours let the bark, drawn over them, cover my dying eyes!”
sentences.i: Take your hands off my eyes: let the closing bark cover my dying eyes, and no last office from you!”
sentences.n: munus here is the last service the living owe the dying, the closing of the eyes, which belonged to the nearest kin — and she refuses it because the bark will do it. inductus is “drawn over”, of a covering pulled across a surface, and contegat is a jussive subjunctive. lumina, “lights”, is the ordinary poetic word for eyes, which makes morientia lumina the lights going out.

sentences.t:
Desierant simul ora loqui, simul esse, diuque
corpore mutato rami caluere recentes.”
sentences.l: Her mouth had ceased at once to speak and at once to be, and long, with her body changed, the new branches stayed warm.
sentences.i: Her lips stopped speaking and stopped existing in the same moment, and long after the body was changed the fresh branches were still warm.
sentences.n: The doubled simul makes one instant do both things: the mouth stops speaking and stops being a mouth. Desierant is pluperfect, so the ending is already behind us when we are told of it. corpore mutato is an ablative absolute, and caluere is caluerunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere. The closing quotation mark ends the tale within the tale.

sentences.t:
Dumque refert Iole factum mirabile, dumque
Eurytidos lacrimas admoto pollice siccat
Alcmene (flet et ipsa tamen), conpescuit omnem
res nova tristitiam.
sentences.l: And while Iole tells the marvellous thing, and while Alcmene, with her thumb applied, dries the tears of Eurytus's daughter — though she is weeping herself too — a new event checked all the sadness.
sentences.i: And while Iole was telling that wonder, and while Alcmene was drying the tears of Eurytus's daughter with her thumb — crying herself all the same — something new put a stop to all the sorrow.
sentences.n: dum with the present indicative refers to past time: “while she was telling”. Eurytidos is a Greek genitive, “of the daughter of Eurytus” — that is Iole herself, so the woman being comforted is the woman who has just told the story. admoto pollice is an ablative absolute, “with the thumb applied”. res nova means a new event rather than a new object, and conpescuit is “penned in, checked”, a word of confining and holding in.

sentences.t:
Nam limine constitit alto
paene puer dubiaque tegens lanugine malas
ora reformatus primos Iolaus in annos.
sentences.l: For on the high threshold stood Iolaus, almost a boy, covering his cheeks with hesitant down, refashioned as to his face into his first years.
sentences.i: For Iolaus was standing in the high doorway, almost a boy again, the first uncertain down on his cheeks and his face made over into its earliest years.
sentences.n: ora reformatus is a Greek accusative of respect: reformatus, “made over”, is the participle, and the accusative ora says in what respect — as to his face. malas, “cheeks”, is the object of tegens, and dubia lanugine is the down of a first beard, “doubtful” because there is barely any of it. The name Iolaus is held off to the end, arriving inside the closing phrase primos ... in annos.

sentences.t:
Hoc illi dederat Iunonia muneris Hebe,
victa viri precibus.
sentences.l: This much of a gift Juno's Hebe had given him, won over by the man's prayers.
sentences.i: Hebe, Juno's own, had given him that much of a gift, won over by a man's prayers.
sentences.n: hoc ... muneris is a partitive genitive, “this much of a gift” — the Latin way of pointing at a gift without measuring it. Iunonia marks Hebe as Juno's, and her gift here is the years just described. victa viri precibus leaves the man unnamed in these lines: the Latin says only that prayers won her over.

sentences.t:
Quae cum iurare pararet
dona tributuram post hunc se talia nulli,
non est passa Themis:
sentences.l: And when she was making ready to swear that she would grant such gifts to no one after him, Themis did not allow it:
sentences.i: And when she was getting ready to swear that she would give gifts like that to nobody after him, Themis would not have it:
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative, “and she”. cum with the imperfect subjunctive pararet gives the circumstance. The oath is an accusative and infinitive with a future infinitive, se ... tributuram (esse), “that she would grant”. non est passa is from patior, deponent (passive in form, active in meaning): Themis did not permit it — and everything from here to the end is her speech.

sentences.t:
“Nam iam discordia Thebae
bella movent” dixit “Capaneusque nisi ab Iove vinci
haud poterit,
sentences.l: “For already Thebes is stirring up wars of discord,” she said, “and Capaneus will not be able to be conquered save by Jove,
sentences.i: “Thebes is already at war with herself,” she said, “and no one but Jove will be able to bring Capaneus down;
sentences.n: discordia is neuter plural and goes with bella, not with Thebae, which would need discordes: the wars are wars of discord. Thebae is plural in Latin, which is why movent is plural with it. nisi and haud are kept apart across the line end and work together: he cannot be conquered, except by Jove. vinci is a passive infinitive with ab Iove as its agent. Capaneus belongs to the war just named, and Themis is prophesying: from here the verbs turn future.

sentences.l: and brothers will be made equal in their wound, and, with the earth pulled away beneath him, the seer, still living, will see his own shades;
sentences.i: and brothers will come out equal in the wound they deal each other, and the ground will be taken from under the prophet and he will look on his own ghost while still alive;
sentences.n: pares in vulnere: each brother's wound matches the other's, which is how they both die — and the Latin does not name them. subducta ... tellure is an ablative absolute, split around suos manes. manes are the shades of the dead, so seeing one's own manes while alive means going down among the dead without dying first. The seer is not named either.

sentences.t:
ultusque parente parentem
natus erit facto pius et sceleratus eodem;
sentences.l: and a son, having avenged a parent by a parent, will be dutiful and criminal by one and the same deed;
sentences.i: and a son will avenge one parent by means of the other, and by that single act be both a dutiful child and a murderer;
sentences.n: parente parentem sets the same noun in two cases side by side — the ablative is the instrument, the accusative the one avenged — and the horror is that both of them are his parents. ultus is from ulciscor, deponent (passive in form, active in meaning): he does the avenging. pius names the duty owed to a father and sceleratus the crime of killing a mother, and facto ... eodem, “by the same deed”, holds the two words together. line 410 says whose shade will hunt him.

sentences.t:
attonitusque malis exsul mentisque domusque,
vultibus Eumenidum matrisque agitabitur umbris,
sentences.l: and, struck senseless by his evils, an exile from his mind and from his house, he will be driven by the faces of the Eumenides and by his mother's shade,
sentences.i: and, stunned by his own evils, driven out of his wits and out of his home, he will be hunted by the faces of the Eumenides and by his mother's ghost,
sentences.n: exsul takes the genitives mentis and domus, which is bold: Latin usually exiles a man from a place, and here the madness and the banishment are made one thing. Eumenides, “the Kindly Ones”, is the placating name given to the avenging spirits, used because naming them outright was dangerous. agitabitur is the verb used of game driven by hunters.

sentences.t:
donec eum coniunx fatale poposcerit aurum,
cognatumque latus Phegeius hauserit ensis.
sentences.l: until his wife shall have demanded of him the fated gold, and a Phegeian sword shall have drained a kinsman's side.
sentences.i: until his wife asks him for the doomed gold, and a sword of Phegeus's house drains the side of a man who is kin to it.
sentences.n: poposcerit takes two accusatives, eum and aurum: Latin demands a thing of a person. haurio of a blade is to drain or drink up, and so to run a body through. Phegeius is an adjective made from a personal name, and cognatum latus says the man run through is kin to those who kill him. Both verbs are future perfect — these things will already have happened when the rest comes true.

sentences.t:
Tum demum magno petet hos Acheloia supplex
ab Iove Callirhoe natis infantibus annos
neve necem sinat esse diu victoris inultam,
sentences.l: Then at last Achelous's daughter Callirhoe, a suppliant, will beg these years from great Jove for her infant sons, and that he not let the killing of the victor be long unavenged,
sentences.i: Then at last Callirhoe, Achelous's daughter, will kneel to great Jove and beg these same years for her infant sons, and beg him not to let the killing of the victor go long unavenged;
sentences.n: hos annos, “these years”, points back to the years given to the young man in the doorway: she asks for the same gift. Acheloia is an adjective from a father's name, “the daughter of Achelous”. petet holds the thing asked (annos), the one asked (ab Iove) and the ones it is for (natis infantibus, dative), and magno is split from its Iove by the line end. neve ... sinat carries the request on as an indirect command. Magnus prints victoris, “of the victor”; some editions print ultoris, “of the avenger”, which would name the dead man by the deed of line 408 instead.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter his motus privignae dona nurusque
praecipiet facietque viros inpubibus annis.”
sentences.l: Jupiter, moved by these things, will take beforehand the gifts of his stepdaughter and son's wife, and will make them men in their unripe years.”
sentences.i: Jupiter, moved by all this, will take in advance the gift that belongs to his stepdaughter and daughter-in-law, and make grown men of children still under age.”
sentences.n: privignae and nurus are two genitives for one person: the giver of youth is at once Jupiter's stepdaughter and his son's wife, which is why the oath at line 402 had to be stopped. praecipiet is “will take in advance” — the gift is hers to grant and his to pre-empt. inpubibus annis is an ablative, “in their unbearded years”, so the children are to skip childhood altogether. The prophecy, and the part, break off at the closing quotation mark.
